evidence.claim: Through Delaware, meetinghouses and a courthouse trace the struggle against slavery.
evidence.quote: Points of Interest State Rt. 10 Agricultural Landscape Camden Friends Meeting House Blackbird State Forest Corbit-Sharp House Dover Green House District Old State House First State Heritage Park New Castle Courthouse Museum Tubman-Garrett Riverfront Park and Market Street Bridge

evidence.claim: The Delaware leg of the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Byway travels north through towns before following Route 9 along the Delaware River to Wilmington.
evidence.quote: The route traverses known Underground Railroad sites in Camden and Dover, continues north on US 13, passing through Smyrna, then continues on Rte 15 to Middletown and Odessa. It then follows Route 9 along the Delaware River to Wilmington

evidence.claim: DelDOT lists this Delaware Byway at approximately 95 miles with its loops and about three hours of driving.
evidence.quote: Length Approximately 95 miles (including the loops) Harriet Tubman Drive Tour Guide Download your driving tour map with directions and information to sites in Maryland, Delaware and Pennsylvania. Drive Time About 3 hours

evidence.claim: The agency presents it as an alternative route through the state, connecting places where Underground Railroad history happened.
evidence.quote: This Byway provides the traveler with an alternative travel route through the state in a generally south to north orientation while giving opportunities to experience Delaware's Underground Railroad history through locations where this history happened.

evidence.claim: Before the Civil War, freedom seekers traveled north through a network of people and landscapes known as the Underground Railroad.
evidence.quote: Before the Civil War, African American Freedom Seekers fled north to freedom through a combination of people and landscapes that became known as the "Underground Railroad."

evidence.claim: In Wilmington, Quaker Thomas Garrett organized members and safe locations.
evidence.quote: Wilmington Quaker, Thomas Garrett, was influential on orchestrating the Underground Railroad network in Delaware through organization of members and safe locations.

evidence.claim: Harriet Tubman repeatedly passed through his station; he supplied lodging, meals, money and shoes for her journeys.
evidence.quote: Garrett was also a friend and benefactor to the noted Underground Railroad Conductor Harriet Tubman, who passed through his station many times. In addition to lodging and meals, Garrett frequently provided her with money and shoes to continue her missions conducting runaways from slavery to freedom.

evidence.claim: Begin where Maryland's byway ends, on Willow Grove Road in Kent County, then continue through Camden and Dover.
evidence.quote: The Byway begins where the Maryland Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Byway ends on Willow Grove Road, Kent County. The route traverses known Underground Railroad sites in Camden and Dover

evidence.claim: US 13 leads through Smyrna, and Route 15 continues to Middletown and Odessa.
evidence.quote: continues north on US 13, passing through Smyrna, then continues on Rte 15 to Middletown and Odessa.

evidence.claim: Route 9 brings the journey to Wilmington and its 13 Underground Railroad sites before Kennett Pike carries the byway to the Pennsylvania line.
evidence.quote: It then follows Route 9 along the Delaware River to Wilmington, where it weaves through 13 Underground Railroad sites. Then it follows Kennett Pike and ends at the Delaware-Pennsylvania State Line.

evidence.claim: Measuring about 20 by 22 feet, the brick meetinghouse in Odessa connects Quaker worship with the Underground Railroad.
evidence.quote: Measuring about 20 feet (6.1 m) by 22 feet (6.7 m), it may be the smallest brick house of worship in the United States.

evidence.claim: Members John Hunn and John Alston took part in the network.
evidence.quote: Members of the meeting, including John Hunn and his cousin John Alston, were active in the Underground Railroad

evidence.claim: Its basement and a loft with a removable panel under the eaves may have sheltered self-liberating Black people.
evidence.quote: The basement and a loft with a removable panel under the eaves may have been used to hide self-liberating Black people.

evidence.claim: After Alston, the last active member, died in 1874, the building deteriorated and was rented to farmers at different times.
evidence.quote: In the early 1870s John Alston was the last active meeting member.  After he died in 1874, the meetinghouse deteriorated. At different times it was rented to local farmers.

evidence.claim: H. Rodney Sharp restored it in 1938, and worship resumed in 1939.
evidence.quote: The building was restored in 1938 by H. Rodney Sharp, opened for worship in 1939

evidence.claim: Quaker worship continues here.
evidence.quote: Worship continues to on a regular basis

evidence.claim: The burial ground has early fieldstones as well as curved-top and modern markers.
evidence.quote: The burial ground behind the meetinghouse includes markers ranging from fieldstones for early Quakers to the curved-top style favored later to more modern markers.

evidence.claim: In 1848, Thomas Garrett and John Hunn faced trial here for violating the Fugitive Slave Act.
evidence.quote: a series of trials which took place in 1848. Prominent abolitionists and Underground Railroad conductors Thomas Garrett (a close friend and ally of Harriet Tubman) and John Hunn were put on trial for violating the Fugitive Slave Act.

evidence.claim: They had helped the family of Emeline and Samuel Hawkins escape slavery.
evidence.quote: In 1848, Garrett and fellow Quaker John Hunn were sued in federal court for helping the Emeline and Samuel Hawkins family of seven slaves owned by two owners escape

evidence.claim: Chief Justice Roger Taney presided, and both men were found guilty.
evidence.quote: The trial was presided over by U.S. Chief Justice Roger Taney.

evidence.claim: Both received heavy fines, yet declared that they would continue helping people escape slavery.
evidence.quote: Both Garrett and Hunn were found guilty and were issued fines heavy enough to bankrupt both men. Despite the fines, Garrett and Hunn defiantly declared they would continue helping slaves escape to freedom.

evidence.claim: The courthouse also shaped a literal boundary: in 1750, a commission agreed to use its cupola as the center of the 12-mile circle.
evidence.quote: A subsequent Commission, including William Allen and Benjamin Chew met in the Court House in 1750, where it was agreed by both sides that the cupola of the Court House building would be used as the center of the 12-mile circle.

evidence.claim: That circle defines most of the Delaware-Pennsylvania border.
evidence.quote: a 12-mile radius that defines most of the border between the states of Delaware and Pennsylvania

evidence.claim: Harriet Tubman, Thomas Garrett and two freedom seekers appear together in a bronze sculpture installed here in 2012.
evidence.quote: In 2012 the bronze sculpture Unwavering Courage in the Pursuit of Freedom by Mario Chiodo was installed in the park, depicting Tubman, Garrett and two freedom seekers

evidence.claim: Mario Chiodo’s work is titled Unwavering Courage in the Pursuit of Freedom.
evidence.quote: the bronze sculpture Unwavering Courage in the Pursuit of Freedom by Mario Chiodo

evidence.claim: The park honors Tubman and Garrett's work together as Underground Railroad operatives in the mid-19th century.
evidence.quote: It is named in honor of Harriet Tubman and Wilmington Quaker abolitionist Thomas Garrett, who worked together as Underground Railroad operatives in the mid-19th century.

evidence.claim: Developed during Wilmington's riverfront revitalization in the late 1990s, the site provided public access to the Christina River.
evidence.quote: The site was developed as part of Wilmington's riverfront revitalization in the late 1990s to provide public access to the Christina River.

evidence.claim: Across from the railroad station, it includes lawns, riverside walkways, historical markers and public art.
evidence.quote: The park is located along Rosa Parks Drive opposite the Joseph R. Biden Jr. Railroad Station and forms part of Wilmington's redeveloped riverfront district. It serves as a venue for concerts, festivals and community events, and includes open lawns, walkways overlooking the river, historical markers and public art.

evidence.claim: The bronze sculpture depicts Tubman, Garrett and two freedom seekers.
evidence.quote: depicting Tubman, Garrett and two freedom seekers

evidence.claim: In 1848, Garrett and fellow Quaker John Hunn were sued for helping the Hawkins family escape. Despite fines, both declared that they would continue their work; the New Castle courthouse joins meetinghouses and commemorative sites along the modern byway.
evidence.quote: In 1848, Garrett and fellow Quaker John Hunn were sued in federal court for helping the Emeline and Samuel Hawkins family of seven slaves owned by two owners escape

evidence.claim: Despite fines, both declared that they would continue their work
evidence.quote: Despite the fines, Garrett and Hunn defiantly declared they would continue helping slaves escape to freedom.

evidence.claim: the New Castle courthouse joins meetinghouses and commemorative sites along the modern byway
evidence.quote: New Castle Courthouse Museum Tubman-Garrett Riverfront Park and Market Street Bridge Wilmington Friends Meeting and Cemetery

evidence.claim: Wilmington Monthly Meeting received title to the property in 2019.
evidence.quote: Wilmington Monthly Meeting was granted title in 2019.

evidence.claim: Delaware opened the courthouse as a museum in 1963.
evidence.quote: The Court House was opened as a museum by the state of Delaware in 1963.

evidence.claim: The public park also serves as a venue for concerts, festivals and community events.
evidence.quote: It serves as a venue for concerts, festivals and community events

evidence.quote: Appoquinimink Friends Meeting House, also known as the Odessa Friends Meetinghouse, is a very small but historic Quaker meetinghouse on Main Street in Odessa, Delaware.
